title: Common definitions
description: Shared primitives referenced by every other schema. Resolved locally; the $id is a stable identifier, not a network location. Nothing in this project fetches a schema at runtime.

domainId.description:
Top-level domain. CM = cross-cutting core, DP = discipline pack organized by measurement QUANTITY, EC = equipment-calibration pack organized by the equipment TYPE that arrives on a bench. Example: CM-03, DP-08, EC-01.

EC exists because the first two axes are both organized by measurement science and neither is organized by the work. Calibrating an oscilloscope is one job that spans DC voltage (DP-08), timing (DP-14) and bandwidth (DP-10); asked to live in a quantity domain it gets truncated to the part that fits, which is exactly what DP-08-052 'Oscilloscope DC and timebase calibration' is.

competencyAreaId.description: Competency area within a domain. Example: CM-03-A02.

elementId.description: Leaf element — the unit of rating, evidence, and credentialing. Example: CM-03-014. IMPORTANT: the domain prefix records where the element was FIRST created and is historical. The authoritative domain and competency area are the `domain` and `competencyArea` fields on the element. If an element is later reassigned, those fields change and the ID does not, because IDs are immutable — a credential attesting CM-03-014 must resolve to the same element forever.

sourceId.description: Key into content/sources/registry.yaml. Example: JCGM-100-2008, ISO-IEC-17025-2017, ASME-Y14-5-2018.

moduleId.description: A training module. Append-only like every other identifier here, because a training record names the module it came from and that has to stay resolvable after the module is retired.

bokArticleId.description: A Body of Knowledge article. Append-only, like every other identifier here: the BOK is meant to be cited by outside work, and a citation that stops resolving is worse than no citation. Deliberately NOT derived from the domain — an article's subject may span domains, and its id must survive being reorganized.

knowledgeRef.description:
A pointer from a competence element to the reference material covering it. Section-level rather than article-level, because the person following it is usually looking for one forgotten detail rather than a topic.

It carries `supports`, the levels of the element it serves, because a pointer that resolves is not a pointer that covers — see that field.

supports.description:
WHICH OF THIS ELEMENT'S LEVELS THIS SECTION SERVES. Required on an element — by `element.schema.json`, not here, because a training module carries knowledgeRefs too and has no rungs of its own to serve; it names an element and a level in `preparesFor` instead. Answers open decision 22.

CI has always proved that a knowledgeRef RESOLVES — the article exists and declares the section. It could never prove the section COVERS what the element assesses, and it still cannot: no check reads prose and decides whether it explains a competence. What changed is that the ABSENCE stopped being invisible. Each ref names the rungs it serves, so the corpus can compute the thing that was actually missing — A LEVEL WITH NO KNOWLEDGE BEHIND IT AND NOBODY SAYING SO.

The worked case is CM-03-052. Its four refs all resolved, all were honest, and its L2 anchor asked a candidate what a reported figure means at a stated coverage factor with no section anywhere in the corpus explaining how to choose and state one. The author knew, and wrote it in a closing note where a human would read it and no code would. Under this field that element cannot be written without either pointing L2 at something or declaring the gap in `knowledgeGaps`.

WHAT IT PROVES AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It proves the author accounted for every attainable level. It does not prove the section covers the level, and an author who writes every rung on every ref without thinking has satisfied the schema and nothing else. That is exactly the standing `positionNeutrality` has, and it is stated for the same reason: what is gained is that a level nobody claimed is now an error instead of a silence.

A level above the element's ceiling is an error — there is no such assessable unit, so nothing can serve it. The shape mirrors `reviews[].covers[].level`, which already answers 'which rungs did somebody actually reach' for review provenance. This asks the same question of knowledge.

It also decides what a credential pins. `pinDefinition` takes the refs serving the level being issued, so a credential at L1 no longer carries — and no longer reports drift against — a section that only ever served L4.

relevance.description: What this section gives the reader of this element. Useful when an element points at several sections across articles.

proof.description:
THE SIGNATURE. Every document in this system that asserts something about somebody carries one, and until 2026-09-20 none of them could hold one.

`proof` required exactly one property, `cryptosuite`, and on three of the four documents that carry it `proof` itself was not required at all. So a credential with NO PROOF OBJECT WHATSOEVER was schema-valid, passed every credential check without a finding, and came back from `verifyAgainstRegistry` with a populated basis that any renderer built against that shape would show as verified. The counter-statement check named 'an unsigned answer is refused' was satisfied by the literal string `ecdsa-jcs-2019` and nothing else.

IT IS THE SAME ERROR AS THE CRYPTOSUITE IDENTIFIER, ONE FIELD OUT. That one was caught, the VALUE was corrected, and the SHAPE around it was never looked at — so the object went on naming a W3C suite it did not have the W3C structure to use. Both are the category the review record names: a claim about the outside world taken on plausibility, about to freeze permanently, invisible to every check here because a `const` is only ever compared with itself.

WHAT THE SPECIFICATION ACTUALLY REQUIRES, read from it rather than recalled. W3C *Verifiable Credential Data Integrity 1.0* §2.1 requires `type` and `proofPurpose`; §4.4 states that verification MUST raise an error if `proof.type`, `proof.verificationMethod` or `proof.proofPurpose` is absent; `proofValue` is the base-encoded binary data without which there is no signature to check. W3C *Data Integrity ECDSA Cryptosuites 1.0* §2.2.1 fixes `type` to `DataIntegrityProof`, §3.3.1 encodes `proofValue` as base58-btc multibase, and §3.3.6 gives the P-256 signature as exactly 64 bytes.

ONE DEFINITION, FOUR DOCUMENTS — credential, counter-statement, disclosure and trust registry. They were four copies of one shape and all four carried the same defect, which is the argument that put `sectionPin`, `person` and the taxonomy selectors here. A verifier that can check a credential and not the registry it resolves against has verified nothing.

THE SHAPE IS NOT THE VERIFICATION. Nothing in this repository verifies a signature yet — see `verifyAgainstRegistry`, which now says so in every verdict it returns. What this object does is make one expressible, so that the contract freezing at Phase 3 is one a signature can be added to without a schema change.

type.description: `DataIntegrityProof`, which W3C *Data Integrity ECDSA Cryptosuites 1.0* §2.2.1 states the type MUST be. It is what makes `cryptosuite` meaningful: the base specification requires `cryptosuite` only when the type is this, so a proof naming a suite without naming its type was asserting a constraint under no rule that reads it.

cryptosuite.description:
The Data Integrity cryptosuite the proof is made under. `ecdsa-jcs-2019` — ECDSA, canonicalized with the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (RFC 8785).

IT SAID `ecdsa-rdfc-2019-p256`, AND NO SUCH SUITE EXISTS. W3C Data Integrity ECDSA Cryptosuites v1.0 defines exactly three identifiers — `ecdsa-rdfc-2019`, `ecdsa-jcs-2019` and `ecdsa-sd-2023` — and the curve is not part of any of them. The value was assembled locally, and it looked entirely plausible: the right suite family, the right curve, joined by a hyphen. Nothing in this repository would ever have caught it, because a `const` is only ever checked against itself. It would have been found by the first person to carry a credential to an implementation that was not ours, which is the one place this project cannot afford to fail — a credential the holder owns is worth what an outside verifier can do with it.

WHY `jcs` AND NOT `rdfc`. This is not a de-hyphenation of the old value; `rdfc` was the wrong half to keep. `ecdsa-rdfc-2019` transforms by converting the document to JSON-LD expanded form, then to RDF statements, then canonicalizing under RDFC-1.0 — which requires an `@context` and the resolution of it. Nothing this project signs is JSON-LD: there is no `@context` on a credential, an authorization or the trust registry, and adding one would pull JSON-LD processing and context resolution into a build whose first constraint is that it makes no external runtime calls. `ecdsa-jcs-2019` canonicalizes the JSON directly under RFC 8785 — no context, no processor, no network. It is the suite that fits both the documents actually signed and the air gap.

WHERE THE P-256 REQUIREMENT WENT. Into `publicKeyMultibase` on the trust registry, which is the only place it can be enforced. The curve is carried by the verification method's Multikey — multicodec `0x1200` for P-256, `0x1201` for P-384 — not by the suite name, so the `-p256` suffix was never load-bearing even if the identifier had been real. The FIPS reasoning behind choosing P-256 over Ed25519 is unchanged and is recorded in `docs/00-context.md`; what changed is that it is now stated somewhere a verifier reads.

Expensive to reverse: every credential already issued is signed with the suite in force at the time. Nothing has been issued, which is why this was correctable at all.

verificationMethod.description:
WHICH KEY SIGNED THIS. Resolved against `keys[].id` on the issuer's trust-registry entry, and required rather than optional because key rotation and compromise are per key: without it a compromised key cannot be told from a sound one, and `verifyAgainstRegistry` can only say so and stop.

Deliberately not patterned. The registry's own `keys[].id` is a free string, and patterning one side of a comparison and not the other is how two fields that must match stop matching. The DID profile a deployment can resolve offline is `didMethods` on the registry, shipped as `did:key` alone.

proofPurpose.description:
`assertionMethod` — and THIS CONSTRAINT IS THIS PROJECT'S, NOT THE SPECIFICATION'S, which is stated here because the last field in this object that quietly asserted a spec requirement it did not have cost a year of being wrong.

The base specification requires the property to exist and does not fix its value; the ECDSA cryptosuite does not prescribe one either, and uses `assertionMethod` in its own credential example (§2.2.1, Example 4). Every document carrying this proof asserts something about somebody — a competence, a revocation answered, a consent granted, a roster of issuers — so none of them is an authentication, and fixing the value makes a mismatch visible. If a later document in this system is genuinely an authentication, this is the field that has to widen, not the one to work around.

proofValue.description:
THE SIGNATURE ITSELF, base58-btc multibase — W3C *Data Integrity ECDSA Cryptosuites 1.0* §3.3.1. Its absence was the whole of the defect: every other field in this object DESCRIBES a signature, and only this one IS one.

THE LENGTH BOUND IS COMPUTED FROM THE ENCODING, AND IS DELIBERATELY WIDER THAN THE COMMON CASE. §3.3.6 gives the P-256 signature as exactly 64 bytes. 64 bytes is log58(2^512) ≈ 87.4 base58 digits, so almost every signature is 87 or 88 characters — but not every one. A value below 58^86 encodes to 86, and base58-btc renders each LEADING ZERO BYTE as a literal `1`, which drives the length lower still, to 64 in the limit.

Measured over 100,000 random 64-byte values: 80.7% at 88 characters, 19.3% at 87, and 0.004% at 86. So a pattern of `{87,88}` — the one that looks right, and the one this field nearly shipped with — would reject roughly one valid signature in 25,000: rare enough never to appear in testing, frequent enough to happen in the field, and undiagnosable by the holder it happens to. The bound here is the full range the encoding can produce for 64 bytes, and the test recomputes the distribution rather than trusting this paragraph.

That is the same discipline as `publicKeyMultibase` on the trust registry and the opposite outcome. There the multicodec header fixes the length exactly, so the pattern is tight and a test recomputes it. Here it cannot be tight, and a tight one would have looked more rigorous while being wrong — which is the failure mode this whole object exists to correct.

sectionPin.description:
One BOK section, pinned by content. An append-only section id keeps the link RESOLVING; only the hash keeps it MEANING what it meant.

Shared because a credential and a preparation record both pin sections, and two definitions of one shape would eventually disagree about what had been pinned.

archetypeId.description: An assessment archetype — a reusable, parameterized item SHAPE, bound to many assessable units. Example: ARC-0007. Archetype IDs are append-only for the same reason element IDs are: a credential records the archetype an item came from, so the provenance of an assessment must stay resolvable after the archetype is retired.

elementKind.description:
What kind of competence this element is, and therefore what evidence proves attainment. knowledge: the person can explain, relate and analyze it — evidence is explanation. skill: the person can perform it — evidence is a work product they actually produced, and an account of how it would be done cannot substitute. judgment: the person can decide under ambiguity and defend the decision — evidence is a defence, and there is often no single right answer.

WHAT CANNOT SUBSTITUTE FOR A SKILL IS DESCRIPTION, NOT WRITING. This said 'a written answer cannot substitute', which over-constrained it: a written artifact is very often the performance itself. An uncertainty budget, a calibration procedure, a method validation report — each is a work product, produced rather than described, and each is the evidence. What cannot stand in is explaining how one WOULD be produced, because that is a knowledge claim wearing a skill's clothes. Whether the performance is observed at a bench or reviewed as a submitted artifact is `demonstration` on the element, and is not decided by `kind`.

The distinction drives assessment design: an L3 knowledge element and an L3 skill element require different evidence, and a uniform ladder across both would test the wrong thing for one of them. RULE: if an element genuinely needs two kinds of evidence, that is a sign it should be two elements. NOTE: authority is deliberately absent from this list. Knowledge, skill and judgment are earned and are properties of a person; authority is granted, and is a relationship between a person, an organization and a scope of work. See docs/00-context.md on competence versus authorization.

proficiencyLevel.description: 1 Novice, 2 Advanced Beginner, 3 Competent, 4 Proficient, 5 Expert.

lifecycleStatus.description: draft: being written. review: awaiting checkpoint approval. stable: approved, safe to assess against. deprecated: superseded, never deleted — see supersededBy.

clauseRef.description: Clause, section, table, or figure within the cited document, as the document itself numbers it. Example: 5.1.2, 7.6.1, Annex F.2.4.5, Table 1. Do not prefix with a section symbol.

citation.description: A precise source reference. Referenceability is universal: every element and every BOK article carries at least one, regardless of the source's licence tier. NOT necessarily a NORMATIVE reference — the corpus covers accepted practice, emerging technique, research and interpretation, and adjacent competencies where no clause requires anything of anybody. What is required is a reference appropriate to the kind of claim; its standing is recorded separately in `currency.authorityStatus`. A citation is a fact and is always permitted; quoting is a separate, tier-gated capability.

edition.description: Edition or year actually consulted, when it differs from the registry default. Omit to inherit the registry entry's edition.

relevance.description: Why this clause matters to this element, in the author's own words. Never a paraphrase so close to the source that it functions as a copy.

quote.description: A typed, attributed quotation — never prose baked into a paragraph. Storing quotes as data is what allows a --strip-tier2 build to remove restricted text mechanically while leaving every citation intact, and what allows `npm run report:quotes` to produce a complete legal-review manifest.

text.description: The quoted words, verbatim and unaltered. Word-count and per-source limits are enforced by the validator against the tier recorded in the source registry, not by this schema — the limits live with the source, so changing a source's terms does not require a schema change.

commentary.description: The author's own analysis of the quoted text. Required by the validator for restricted-tier quotations: a quotation must accompany commentary, never substitute for the clause.

organizationRef.description:
An organization, named and where possible identified. Used wherever the difference between two organizations has to be DECIDED rather than displayed — the cross-organizational signer rule at L5, and reciprocal-review detection.

WHY THIS IS NOT A STRING. It was one, and the rule that rests on it — 'at least one signer outside the candidate's own organization, so that a closed group cannot certify its own experts' — was therefore only as strong as string inequality. Two colleagues at one laboratory writing 'Northfield Calibration' and 'Northfield Calibration Ltd' satisfied it. That is a defect with plausible deniability: it looks like a formatting difference and works like an evasion.

`id` settles identity; `name` is compared after normalization when no id is present. Normalization collapses case, punctuation and trailing legal suffixes, which catches the accidental variant. It does NOT catch an abbreviation or a deliberate rename, and the validator says which comparison it used rather than claiming more than it proved.

name.description: The organization as it calls itself. Always present, because a reader needs something legible even when no identifier exists.

id.description: A stable identifier — a trust-registry key, or the organization's DID. Optional on purpose: requiring one would mean a signer whose laboratory has never issued anything could not sign, which gates participation behind registration and is the barrier this project refuses. Supplying one is what turns a nominal comparison into an identity comparison.

contentRef.description: Content-addressed reference to an archived artifact. Hashing is what makes a credential re-reviewable years later.

taxonomyIncludes.description:
What is in scope, resolved against the taxonomy. Selectors are unioned, and every value names a domain, an area or an element that the taxonomy either contains or does not — which is what makes a scope MACHINE-RESOLVABLE rather than a description somebody has to read.

Shared between a deployment scope and an authorization scope deliberately. They answer different questions — which elements apply to this person's job, and which measurement work this grant covers — but both are resolved by the same operation against the same taxonomy, and two implementations of "is this element inside this selector set" would disagree eventually.

elements.description: Individually named elements, for the case the work crosses a boundary the taxonomy draws elsewhere.

taxonomyExcludes.description:
Removed after the includes are unioned. For the common case of "this whole domain except the part we send out to a subcontractor".

There is deliberately no `domains` here. Excluding a whole domain you had to include first is a longer way of not including it, and permitting both spellings would leave two scopes that read differently and resolve identically.

reviewerStanding.description:
How a reader can satisfy themselves that this reviewer was in a position to review this. Two of the three bases RESOLVE and one does not, and telling them apart is the entire point of the field.

`reviewer` is a name and an optional DID. Without this, the corpus could establish that X reviewed a section on a date and could not establish that X had any standing to — the exact gap decision 47 closed for credential signers, where an unbacked `heldLevel: 4` stopped counting as evidence of anything. The same rule had never been applied to the people reviewing the corpus itself.

It cannot PROVE the third case, and nothing could. What it does is stop the three being indistinguishable.

basis.description:
`held-credential` — the reviewer holds a credential in this system, named and pinned by content. A reader resolves it offline exactly as they resolve any other credential. EVIDENCED, and it requires both `credentialId` and `credentialRef`: claiming the resolvable basis without the thing that resolves it is the overstatement `provenanceTier` already refuses.

`founding-cohort` — the reviewer sits on the published founding cohort, which a reader resolves against `content/competence/bootstrap-cohort.yaml` the same way a verifier does. EVIDENCED, and it requires the reviewer's `did` to appear on that roster. The shipped roster convenes nobody, so this basis resolves for no one today — the correct state while steward appointment is outstanding, and the same answer every other roster-backed claim gives.

`stated` — external standing described in prose: practice, publication, a post held. A reader WEIGHS it rather than resolving it, exactly as they weigh the name of a reviewer on a paper. ASSERTED, and honest about being so. It is the only basis available while nobody holds a credential and the cohort is empty, which is why it exists and why it is not second-class.

credentialId.description: The credential the reviewer holds. Named rather than described, so a reader can go and look.

credentialRef.description: That credential pinned by content, so the standing cannot be claimed from a credential that has since been revised.

statement.description: What the standing IS, for a `stated` basis. Long enough to be weighable: 'twenty years in dimensional calibration, UKAS technical assessor' tells a reader something, and 'expert' does not.

person.description:
A named human. `name` rather than only a DID because the people who review this corpus are practitioners whose names carry weight in the field, and a bare identifier tells a reader nothing. The DID is optional and links the person to their own credentials where they hold them.

Shared between articles and elements deliberately. It lived on `bok-article` alone, and an element had no way to name anybody at all — which is how an element could be marked as the exemplar others are held to with nobody recorded as having written it and nobody recorded as having read it.
